The frame: the data link layer's envelope

When a station sends a message onto the medium, it does so using the Ethernet frame format: the envelope in which the data link layer puts what it receives from the network layer.

The envelope has a header, with the elements the protocol needs to operate, and a trailer at the end.

The figure in the notes draws it reversed (preamble on the right) because the arrow shows the direction of transmission: the first thing to go onto the cable is the preamble.
It is the same frame format from the original 10 Mbps up to 10 Gb.
Header: from the preamble to Len/Type · Payload: data + padding · Trailer: FCS. The numbers are the size of each field in bytes.
Preamble and SFD: preparing the receiver

The first two fields carry no information: they prepare the stations that are listening.

  • Preamble (7 bytes): gets all the stations to synchronize. Originally the Manchester code was used, which guarantees a transition in every time interval.
  • SFD, Start of Frame Delimiter (1 byte): marks the end of the preamble and the start of the frame.
First 7 bytes to lock onto the sender's rhythm; then 1 byte that signals that what follows is already the frame.
DA and SA: who it goes to and who sent it

Next come the two addresses, 6 bytes each:

  • DA (Destination Address): the destination address.
  • SA (Source Address): the source address.

These are the MAC addresses: 48-bit addresses tied to the network interface. Every device with a network card comes with its MAC from the factory, and that address is unique: it is never repeated.
The destination comes first: it is the first thing the receiver of the frame needs to look at.
DA and SA are 6 bytes = 48 bits each. A MAC is written in hexadecimal, for example 00-12-F0-22-1C-76.

The MAC address is made up of two halves:

  • OUI: unique identifier of the manufacturer.
  • DUI: unique identifier of the device.

Addresses are regulated by the IEEE: it assigns an OUI block to each manufacturer, and the manufacturer assigns a DUI to each of its devices.
The IEEE hands out the OUIs, each manufacturer hands out its DUIs: that way no MAC is ever repeated.
In 00-12-F0-22-1C-76, the 00-12-F0 half says who made the card and 22-1C-76 which card it is.
Unicast: is this frame for me?

The frame propagates through the medium and all stations receive it. Each one decides what to do by looking at the DA:

  • If it is equal to its MAC, it receives and processes it.
  • If it is different, it ignores and discards it.

This is unicast: there is one source and one destination, the sender sends a message to the recipient. In the animation, A writes to C.
The medium is shared, but addressing makes only the recipient keep the frame.
Each station first checks the CRC (FCS field). If it is correct, it compares the DA with its own MAC: only C processes it.

There are special addresses. The broadcast one is filled with all ones: 48 bits set to 1, which in hexadecimal is written FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF.

That destination address indicates that the message is directed to all the stations on the network: all of them receive it and process it.
Broadcast = «for everyone». It shows up again in every lesson that follows: bridges, switches and VLANs.
FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF = 48 bits set to one. No station discards it.

In multicast the message is directed to a group of recipients: there is a MAC address that identifies the group.

A station receives and processes that frame only if it is in the group.

So each station checks whether the DA is:

  • unicast and it is the recipient,
  • broadcast, or
  • multicast for a group it belongs to.
B and D belong to the group and process it. C receives it anyway, but discards it.

After the addresses comes a 2-byte field that means different things depending on the standard:

  • In Ethernet II it is Type (or ethertype): it indicates the protocol that requested the transmission, so the data can be handed to it at the destination. For example, IPv4.
  • In 802.3 it is Length: it contains the length of the data field.
Same place and same size in both versions: that is why the field is called Len/Type.
The rest of the frame is identical. The only thing that changes is how this field is interpreted: who to hand the data to (Type) or how many bytes of data there are (Length).
Data, PAD and FCS: the end of the frame

• Data: from 0 to 1500 bytes. It is the message delivered by the network layer.
  • PAD: from 0 to 46 bytes of padding. If the frame does not reach the 64-byte minimum set by the standard (the collision window), the data link layer fills in what is missing.
  • FCS, Frame Check Sequence: 4 bytes with a 32-bit CRC. Each station checks it before looking at the destination address.
PAD guarantees the minimum size; FCS lets you detect that the frame arrived damaged.
Minimum: 6 + 6 + 2 + 10 of data + 36 of padding + 4 = 64 bytes. Maximum: 6 + 6 + 2 + 1500 + 4 = 1518 bytes. With 46 bytes of data or more, the PAD is 0.

• Preamble + SFD (7 + 1): synchronize and mark the start.
  • DA and SA (6 + 6): 48-bit MAC addresses, OUI + DUI.
  • The DA can be unicast, broadcast (all ones) or multicast (a group).
  • Len/Type (2): protocol in Ethernet II, length in 802.3.
  • Data + PAD: up to 1500 bytes, with padding to reach 64.
  • FCS (4): 32-bit CRC.

How is a MAC address composed?
48 bits chosen at random by each station
The IEEE assigns an OUI block to each manufacturer and the manufacturer a DUI to each device: 24 + 24 = 48 bits.
A frame arrives with destination address FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF. Which stations process it?
None: it is an invalid address
Only the one with that factory MAC
Only those that belong to a group
All ones is the broadcast address: it is directed to all stations, which receive and process it.
In Ethernet II, what does the 2-byte field after the source address indicate?
The length of the data field
The protocol that requested the transmission (e.g., IPv4)
In Ethernet II it is Type or ethertype; in 802.3 that same field contains the length of the data.
The network layer delivers only 10 bytes of data. What does the data link layer do?
Discards the message for being too short
Fills in with 36 bytes of PAD to reach 64 bytes
The standard requires a 64-byte minimum; the PAD field (0 to 46 bytes) fills in what is missing: 6 + 6 + 2 + 10 + 36 + 4 = 64.
7 bytes so the stations synchronize + 1 byte that marks the end of the preamble and the start of the frame.
Destination and source address, 6 bytes each. They are MAC addresses.
48 bits, unique, from the factory. OUI (manufacturer, assigned by the IEEE) + DUI (device, assigned by the manufacturer).
One recipient · all stations (48 ones, FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF) · a group identified by a MAC.
